title: Gram-Positive Cocci: Catalase, Coagulase and MRSA
summary: Follow purple grapes from a blood culture through three forks — catalase bubbles, a coagulase clot and the cefoxitin gate — and see how mecA’s PBP2a defeats β-lactams.

reviewer.note: Teaches Ch. 57 Hit 1 (core: mecA → PBP2a), Hits 2, 3, 21 and 22 (catalase and coagulase forks), Traps 2 and 3 and the Figure 57 memory anchor. Methods are checked against the ASM catalase and coagulase protocols and the CDC MRSA laboratory page; S. lugdunensis details against Shah 2010 and Heilbronner 2020.

objectives: Use catalase to separate staphylococci from streptococci and enterococci, and name its false positives.
Contrast slide (bound) and tube (free) coagulase, and state which is definitive.
Explain how mecA and PBP2a cause MRSA and how labs detect it, including the S. lugdunensis breakpoint rule.

scenes.title: Purple grapes in a blood culture
scenes.altText: A blood-culture bottle flags positive. A Gram-stain field shows purple (Gram-positive) cocci in grape-like clusters. Two question tokens appear: “S. aureus or a skin coagulase-negative staph?” and “MRSA?”. The cartoon scientist looks at three test tokens: catalase, coagulase, cefoxitin.

cues.text: A blood culture turns positive. The Gram stain shows purple cocci in clusters, like bunches of grapes.
Two questions matter at once. Is it Staphylococcus aureus, a dangerous pathogen, or a skin staph that is often a contaminant? And is it MRSA?
Three tests answer them in order: catalase, coagulase and cefoxitin.

props.label: Gram stain: Gram-positive cocci in clusters

scenes.title: Fork 1: catalase
scenes.altText: Two drops of 3% hydrogen peroxide on a slide. Clustered purple cocci (staphylococci) are added to the left drop and it fizzes with oxygen bubbles: catalase positive. Chained purple cocci (streptococci) are added to the right drop and nothing happens: catalase negative. An equation token shows 2 H₂O₂ → 2 H₂O + O₂. A caution card warns that red cells carried over from blood agar have catalase and can give a false positive, and that a platinum loop can too.

cues.text: Catalase is the first fork for Gram-positive cocci. Catalase breaks hydrogen peroxide into water and oxygen gas.
Mix a staph colony into a drop of peroxide and it fizzes with oxygen bubbles. Staphylococci, and Micrococcus, are catalase positive.
Streptococci and enterococci, which grow in chains and pairs, give no bubbles. They are catalase negative.
Watch for false positives. Red cells have their own catalase, so don’t scoop blood agar along with the colony.
And don’t drop peroxide onto a platinum loop: platinum can make bubbles too. A nichrome loop or a wooden stick is fine.

props.title: False positive: red cells from blood agar carry catalase
lines: Platinum loop + peroxide can bubble too → use nichrome or a wooden stick

scenes.title: Fork 2: coagulase — slide and tube
scenes.altText: Left: a slide drop of EDTA rabbit plasma; scattered purple cocci pull together into visible clumps within seconds — bound coagulase (clumping factor) grabbing fibrinogen. Right: a tube of plasma with cocci mixed in; a timeline runs 0 → 4 h at 35–37 °C, then room temperature to 24 h, and the plasma sets into a clot — free coagulase (staphylocoagulase) activating prothrombin. A card: slide is fast but can be falsely negative; tube is the definitive test. A small note: S. lugdunensis and S. schleiferi may clump on the slide; S. schleiferi and S. intermedius may clot the tube.

cues.text: Fork two separates Staphylococcus aureus from coagulase-negative staphylococci. There are two different coagulase tests.
The slide test looks for bound coagulase, also called clumping factor. It grabs fibrinogen in plasma and the cells clump within about 10 seconds.

The tube test looks for free coagulase, which the bacteria secrete into plasma. It activates prothrombin and the plasma clots. Read over 4 hours at 35 to 37 degrees; if there is no clot, leave it at room temperature and read again at 24 hours.
The slide test is fast but can be falsely negative. The tube test is the definitive one, so a negative slide goes on to a tube.
Neither test is unique to Staphylococcus aureus. S. lugdunensis and S. schleiferi may clump on the slide, and S. schleiferi and S. intermedius may clot the tube.

props.title: Slide = fast, can be falsely negative · Tube = definitive
lines: Negative slide → do the tube test

props.label: Not unique to S. aureus: slide + in S. lugdunensis, S. schleiferi · tube + in S. schleiferi, S. intermedius

scenes.title: Fork 3: mecA, PBP2a and cefoxitin
scenes.altText: A schematic cell wall: β-lactam keys (penicillin, cephalosporin, carbapenem) slot into normal PBP locks and the wall-building stops. Then a gene token “mecA” produces a new lock, PBP2a, whose slot the keys don’t fit; wall-building continues — MRSA. A ceftaroline key is shown fitting PBP2a. A testing panel lists cefoxitin disk diffusion or broth microdilution, oxacillin broth microdilution, PBP2a latex, and mecA PCR (misses mecC), with “incubate 35 ± 2 °C; hotter can miss MRSA”.

cues.text: Beta-lactam drugs work by jamming penicillin-binding proteins, the enzymes that build the cell wall.
MRSA carries the mecA gene. It makes a different penicillin-binding protein, PBP2a, that beta-lactams bind poorly, so the wall keeps being built.
Result: resistance to most beta-lactams, including cephalosporins and carbapenems. The exception is ceftaroline, a cephalosporin that does bind PBP2a.
To detect it, labs use cefoxitin disk diffusion or broth microdilution, or oxacillin broth microdilution. PBP2a latex tests and mecA PCR are added tools, but PCR misses the rarer mecC gene.
Incubate at 35 plus or minus 2 degrees. Hotter incubation may miss some MRSA, because resistance can be expressed by only part of the population.

props.title: PBP2a
lines: β-lactams bind poorly → wall keeps building

props.title: Detect MRSA
lines: Cefoxitin disk or broth MIC · oxacillin broth MIC

scenes.title: Two classic traps
scenes.altText: Trap card: “Slide coagulase negative = not S. aureus” is crossed out → “The slide can be falsely negative; confirm with the tube test.” Trap card: “S. lugdunensis is a CoNS, so use CoNS breakpoints” is crossed out → “It behaves like S. aureus (destructive endocarditis); CLSI groups it with S. aureus for oxacillin and cefoxitin.” An example: oxacillin MIC 1 µg/mL reads resistant for CoNS but susceptible for S. lugdunensis. Clue tokens: PYR +, ornithine decarboxylase +.

cues.text: Trap one: a negative slide coagulase does not rule out Staphylococcus aureus. The slide misses some strains, so do the tube test.
Trap two: S. lugdunensis is coagulase negative but behaves like S. aureus, including destructive endocarditis. Its oxacillin and cefoxitin results are read with the S. aureus breakpoints.
That changes answers: an oxacillin MIC of 1 reads resistant for other coagulase-negative staph, but susceptible for S. lugdunensis.
Its bench clues: it may clump on the slide but not clot the tube, and it is PYR and ornithine decarboxylase positive.

props.title: ✗ “Slide coagulase negative = not S. aureus.”
lines: ✓ Slide can be falsely negative → tube test

props.title: ✗ “S. lugdunensis is a CoNS → CoNS breakpoints.”
lines: ✓ Read oxacillin/cefoxitin with S. aureus breakpoints

props.label: S. lugdunensis clues: slide ± / tube − · PYR + · ornithine +

scenes.title: Bubbles → clot → cefoxitin gate
scenes.altText: Memory aid: a three-step path. Step 1, a fizzing drop (“Bubbles: staph”). Step 2, a clotted tube (“Clot: aureus”). Step 3, a gate labelled cefoxitin with a mecA padlock (“Gate: MRSA?”). A card lists where the aid breaks.

cues.text: Memory aid: bubbles, then clot, then the cefoxitin gate. Bubbles say staph, a tube clot says aureus, and cefoxitin tells you whether mecA has locked out the beta-lactams.
Where it breaks: blood agar or a platinum loop can fake bubbles, a few other staph species can clot or clump, S. lugdunensis is clot-negative yet read like aureus, and mecC can slip past a mecA PCR.

props.title: Where it breaks
lines: Blood agar or platinum loop fake bubbles · other staph can clump or clot
S. lugdunensis: clot − but read like aureus · mecC escapes mecA PCR

scenes.title: Takeaway
scenes.altText: Three tokens: “Catalase +: staph · catalase −: strep/enterococcus”, “Tube coagulase is definitive for S. aureus”, “mecA → PBP2a = MRSA; detect with cefoxitin”.

cues.text: Catalase splits staph from strep, the tube coagulase confirms Staphylococcus aureus, and mecA-made PBP2a — detected with cefoxitin — makes it MRSA.

props.label: Tube coagulase is the definitive S. aureus test
mecA → PBP2a = MRSA · detect with cefoxitin

explanation.what: Plain language: purple cocci in clusters are usually staph; three bench steps tell you which staph and whether common antibiotics will fail. Scientific terms: catalase (2H₂O₂ → 2H₂O + O₂) separates catalase-positive staphylococci and Micrococcus from catalase-negative streptococci and enterococci; coagulase separates S. aureus from coagulase-negative staphylococci (CoNS); MRSA carries mecA, encoding PBP2a.
explanation.why: β-lactams kill by binding penicillin-binding proteins that cross-link the cell wall. PBP2a has low affinity for them, so wall synthesis continues: MRSA resists most β-lactams, including cephalosporins and carbapenems, except ceftaroline. Bound coagulase (clumping factor) binds fibrinogen and clumps cells; free coagulase (staphylocoagulase) activates prothrombin and clots plasma.
explanation.measure: Catalase with 3% H₂O₂ (avoid red-cell carry-over and platinum loops). Slide coagulase in EDTA rabbit plasma (clumps within ~10 s); tube coagulase read over 4 h at 35–37 °C, then room temperature to 24 h. MRSA: cefoxitin disk diffusion or broth microdilution, oxacillin broth microdilution, PBP2a latex, mecA PCR; incubate at 35 ± 2 °C.
explanation.differs: Slide (bound coagulase, fast, can be falsely negative) vs tube (free coagulase, definitive). S. lugdunensis is a CoNS but its oxacillin/cefoxitin results use S. aureus breakpoints; other CoNS have their own, lower oxacillin breakpoints.
explanation.examAngle: Expect: catalase results by genus, the false-positive catalase from blood agar, slide vs tube coagulase, mecA/PBP2a and the ceftaroline exception, cefoxitin as the MRSA surrogate, and S. lugdunensis read with S. aureus breakpoints.

comparisons.title: Slide vs tube coagulase

left.label: Slide
points: Can be falsely negative; may be + in S. lugdunensis, S. schleiferi

right.label: Tube
points: 4 h at 35–37 °C, then room temperature to 24 h
Definitive; may be + in S. schleiferi, S. intermedius

comparisons.distinguisher: Cell-bound clumping in seconds vs secreted enzyme clotting plasma over hours.

right.label: Catalase −
points: Chains and pairs on Gram stain

mnemonic.explanation: Bubbles (catalase) say staph, a tube clot (coagulase) says S. aureus, and cefoxitin tests whether mecA’s PBP2a has locked out the β-lactams.
mnemonic.limitation: Red cells and platinum loops fake bubbles; S. schleiferi and S. intermedius can clot or clump; S. lugdunensis does not clot the tube yet is read with S. aureus breakpoints; mecC escapes mecA PCR; and some MRSA show resistance in only part of the population.

analogyLimitations: Keys and locks for β-lactams and PBPs simplify enzyme binding.
Drawn cocci, bubbles and clumps are schematic — not real Gram-stain morphology or reaction strength.
The oxacillin MIC example applies current CLSI-style breakpoints; check the current M100 edition.
takeaway: Catalase splits staph from strep, the tube coagulase confirms Staphylococcus aureus, and mecA-made PBP2a — detected with cefoxitin — makes it MRSA.

questions.stem: Gram-positive cocci in clusters from a blood-agar colony give vigorous bubbles when mixed with 3% H₂O₂. The technologist had scraped some agar with the colony. What is the best interpretation?

options.text: Repeat without agar — red cells in blood agar contain catalase and can cause a false positive
options.rationale: Correct. Carry-over of red cells from blood agar can produce bubbles regardless of the organism.

options.text: Report Streptococcus, because bubbles mean catalase negative
options.rationale: Incorrect. Bubbles mean catalase positive; streptococci are catalase negative.

options.text: Report S. aureus, because catalase positive identifies it
options.rationale: Incorrect. Catalase only separates staphylococci (and Micrococcus) from streptococci; coagulase is needed for S. aureus.
Incorrect. Enterococci are catalase negative, and the result itself is unreliable here.

questions.stem: A catalase-positive, clustered GPC is slide-coagulase negative. What should be done next to decide whether it is S. aureus?

options.rationale: Correct. The slide test can be falsely negative; the tube test (free coagulase) is definitive.
Incorrect. A negative slide alone does not rule out S. aureus.
Incorrect. Catalase does not separate S. aureus from other staphylococci.
Incorrect. Cefoxitin predicts methicillin resistance; it does not identify the species.

questions.stem: Why is an MRSA isolate resistant to oxacillin and cefazolin?

options.text: mecA encodes PBP2a, which has low affinity for β-lactams
options.rationale: Correct. PBP2a keeps building cell wall when other PBPs are blocked; ceftaroline is the cephalosporin exception that binds it.
Incorrect. ESBLs are a Gram-negative mechanism; methicillin resistance in staphylococci is PBP2a.
Incorrect. Staphylococci have a thick peptidoglycan wall; that is why they stain Gram-positive.

options.text: It pumps β-lactams out with an efflux pump
options.rationale: Incorrect. Efflux is not the mechanism of methicillin resistance.

references.citation: Heilbronner S, Foster TJ. Staphylococcus lugdunensis: a skin commensal with invasive pathogenic potential. Clin Microbiol Rev. 2020;34(2):e00205-20.
references.usedFor: S. lugdunensis is a CoNS causing serious infections akin to S. aureus, including destructive infective endocarditis; often misidentified as S. aureus before MALDI-TOF MS.

claims.text: Catalase separates catalase-positive staphylococci/Micrococcus from catalase-negative streptococci; red-cell carry-over and platinum loops can give false positives.
Slide = bound coagulase (clumping factor), ~10 s, can be falsely negative; tube = free coagulase, definitive, 4 h then room temperature to 24 h; other species may be slide- or tube-positive.

MRSA resists most β-lactams including cephalosporins and carbapenems except ceftaroline; detected by cefoxitin (disk or broth), oxacillin broth, PBP2a latex, mecA PCR (misses mecC); incubate 35 ± 2 °C.
mecA encodes PBP2a, which has low affinity for β-lactams.
claims.note: The CDC page read names mecA, mecC and PBP2a testing but does not describe PBP2a affinity; a primary source is still needed.

claims.text: S. lugdunensis: CoNS with S. aureus-like invasive disease; slide +/tube −; PYR and ornithine +; oxacillin/cefoxitin read with S. aureus breakpoints.

claims.note: Not taught; the ASM protocol calls the tube test definitive without a sensitivity figure. See register flag rv-coag-tube-sensitivity.

claims.text: Keys and locks, bubbles, clumps and drawn cocci.

accuracyFlags.issue: The reviewer gives the tube coagulase as “~100% sensitive”; no source read gives a figure, so the lesson says only “definitive”.
Hit 3 reads “positive = S. aureus”; ASM notes S. schleiferi and S. intermedius may also be tube-positive. The lesson teaches the exceptions.

morphology.note: Cocci, bubbles, clumps and clots are schematic drawings, not real Gram-stain or reaction images.
